content: The reporting of diagnostic tests is highly variable. Blood tests for glucose and sodium are not routinely required for all children with febrile seizures, as stated by multiple authorities. A study of British children presenting with a first febrile seizure found that only 1 in 269 had hypoglycemia, while 8% had hyperglycemia. The diagnostic yield of blood cultures in children with febrile seizures is not significantly different from that obtained in pediatric emergency departments. For children presenting with acute convulsive seizures, guidelines recommend checking blood glucose levels, as this can significantly improve diagnostic outcomes. Shah et al. (2014) evaluated the value of blood glucose measurement in children with seizures before hospital admission and made a weak recommendation to check glucose in children presenting with convulsive seizures or status epilepticus. They noted that the evidence was of low to very low quality but strongly recommended treating hypoglycemia diagnosed before hospital arrival with dextrose or glucagon. Expert guidelines recommend testing blood sodium only if there are signs of dehydration or severe diarrhea. A prospective study in Nigeria involving 522 children aged 1 month to 6 years with fever and convulsions found bacterial meningitis in 13 cases. The authors concluded that bacterial meningitis occurs in a reasonable proportion of children with acute febrile seizures, even beyond infancy, and that the decision to perform lumbar puncture should be guided by clinical features. In resource-poor countries with a high incidence of serious CNS infections, lumbar puncture may be indicated in children presenting with fever and seizures. A study in Iran involving 111 children with febrile seizures identified four cases of bacterial meningitis. Studies of varying validity have been conducted to determine the probability of meningitis in hospital settings. The evidence was rated as Level III, with a Delphi consensus and a Grade C recommendation. The diagnostic yield of lumbar puncture in these cases could significantly improve outcomes. Electroencephalography (EEG) is not recommended for children with simple or complex febrile seizures due to variability in patient selection, seizure causes, and timing of EEG after the seizure. Guidelines on EEG use for first seizure presentations vary depending on the clinical presentation. In lowand middle-income countries, obtaining an EEG can be challenging. Neuroimaging, such as CT or MRI, is recommended only if there is altered consciousness or focal neurological signs. MRI is more sensitive than CT, but both are often unavailable in resource-limited settings. The reviewed guidelines recommend neuroimaging in cases of acute convulsive seizures with altered consciousness or focal neurological signs, as it can influence management by identifying complications or aiding in diagnosis. Skull X-rays are not useful for diagnosing febrile seizures. The benefits of diagnostic tests, such as blood tests and lumbar puncture, outweigh the potential harms, even though the evidence quality is low. These tests provide valuable information for excluding infectious causes of seizures and guiding management. However, lumbar punctures can cause morbidity and, in rare cases, death from herniation. Parents and healthcare providers may have differing preferences regarding these tests, with some parents hesitant about lumbar punctures due to fear of distressing the child. Resource requirements for diagnostic tests, such as blood and urine cultures, lumbar punctures, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis, may not be available in many lowand middle-income healthcare facilities. Neuroimaging is often limited by cost and availability. Feasibility depends on training clinical staff to perform and interpret these tests and ensuring their availability in healthcare facilities. Implementation of these guidelines requires revising existing WHO publications relevant to critically ill infants and children. WHO will work with ministries of health and partners to train healthcare workers and adapt recommendations to local contexts. Successful implementation depends on participatory consensus and adaptation to national guidelines. Monitoring and evaluation should be integrated into implementation to assess the impact of recommendations on care quality. Future research priorities include determining the usefulness of neuroimaging and other diagnostic tests in acute seizures or altered consciousness, particularly in resource-limited settings. WHO will monitor guideline implementation and update recommendations as new evidence becomes available.
